messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rafael Morales is a 75-year-old Mexican American man who has spent most of his adult life as a QA engineer, a role he still works in part time from a quiet office on the edge of a manufacturing floor. He traces the start of his current difficulties to a wildfire three years ago, when hot, wind-driven flames raced through the dry hills behind his neighborhood. That afternoon the air had turned strange before he understood why: a heavy burnt smell pushed into the house, the sky took on an orange cast, and ash moved past the windows like gray snow. By evening he could see flames cresting the ridge. He remembers standing in the driveway with his wife, frozen for a moment by the sight of the fireline and the sound of helicopters overhead, before they left with only a few belongings. What remains sharpest for him is not a complete story but sensory fragments: the smell of smoke in his throat, the glow reflected on nearby houses, and the hot, windy weather that made it feel as if the whole landscape had become unsafe.

In the months afterward, those same cues began to take on outsized force. If someone lit a grill nearby, if he passed a roadside burn pile, or if the late summer air became dry and gusty in the way it had that day, Rafael felt his body react before he could think. His chest tightened, his heart kicked hard, and he became instantly alert to exits, windows, and any sign of danger. At work, even a faint electrical smell on the manufacturing floor could make him stop mid-task and scan the room. When he caught sight of flames on a television in a waiting room or saw wildfire footage online, he startled violently and found himself unable to settle for hours. Similar weather now changes the whole tone of his day; when the wind rises and the sky looks washed out, he is on guard from morning onward, listening for sirens and checking outside repeatedly as if danger might already be approaching.

These moments do not pass cleanly. Once smoke, flames, or that particular weather catches his attention, Rafael turns inward and begins circling the same thoughts. He dwells on what he should have done differently and replays the day in a punishing way: he should have packed sooner, should have recognized the danger earlier, should have protected his wife better. Just as often he gets stuck trying to solve the disaster after the fact, mentally rehearsing how it could have been prevented, whether he could have cleared more brush, whether anyone could have stopped the fire before it reached the neighborhood. He knows these thoughts go nowhere, but he also tries to force them away, telling himself not to think about the fire, pushing the images and questions down whenever they arise.

The more physically on edge he feels, the more urgently he tries to control his mind. After a day of being superalert, he goes to bed exhausted but mentally busy, determined not to let himself think about smoke or flames. That effort tends to sharpen the very material he is trying to banish. He becomes aware of every creak in the house and startles at small noises, and in that keyed-up state he returns to the same self-blaming review of the evacuation and the same futile analysis of how the fire might have been prevented. He has come to believe that if he lets his guard down, he will miss the first sign of another disaster; at the same time, he criticizes himself for still reacting this strongly, which keeps the mental churn going.

Over time, this has narrowed his world. In the QA lab he now notices smells before anyone else does and checks them repeatedly, even when coworkers are unconcerned. If a monitor displays fire in a test video or a news alert mentions wildfires, his body surges again and he cannot pull his attention back. Afterward he tries even harder to suppress the images, but this seems to leave him more sensitized to the next whiff of smoke or glimpse of flame, as though his mind is primed to detect exactly what he is trying not to notice. His wife has begun to comment on how quickly weather changes overtake him: a warm, windy afternoon can make him pace from room to room, scanning the horizon and flinching at ordinary sounds.

Rafael finally agreed to seek help after a recent incident at work, when the smell of overheated wiring sent him into such a strong physical reaction that he had to leave the floor and sit in his car, shaken and ashamed. He was troubled not only by how intense the reaction was, but by how quickly it drew him back into the old spiral of blame and mental rehearsal. What frightens him most is the sense that his body now acts as if the fire is always about to return, and that every effort to master the memories only makes smoke, flames, and certain weather feel more powerful. What he hopes for, quietly, is to be able to smell summer air or see fire on a screen without feeling that his whole system has been pulled back to that hillside again.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers creating a sense of danger, but it does not clearly state that Rafael’s threat perception itself increases his attention to or detection of triggers/reminders.

The vignette implies that feeling on edge is followed by efforts to control his mind, but it does not clearly frame the sense of threat itself as causing maladaptive strategies such as avoidance, suppression, or safety behaviours.
